title: The Sound of Persuasion: Using Generative AI to Identify Gender Gaps in Political Influence
authors: Ethan C. Busby, Lisa P. Argyle, Parker Davis, Joshua R. Gubler, Bryce Hepner, Christopher F. Karpowitz, Alex Lyman, Justin Olcott, Jessica R. Preece, and David Wingate
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (forthcoming)
summary: Using real-time conversations with AI agents, this study separates voice-based gender cues from persuasive rhetoric and the topic of discussion. In this experiment, male- and female-sounding voices did not differ directly in persuasiveness; topic and participant gender were associated with differences in persuasion. The findings identify specific gender-related dynamics rather than establishing that gender bias is absent from political conversation.

title: Looking Under the Hood: How LLMs Attempt Political Persuasion and Microtargeting
authors: Alex Lyman, Ethan C. Busby, Lisa P. Argyle, Joshua R. Gubler, Bryce Hepner, and David Wingate
summary: Examining how language models construct generic and customized political messages, this study finds that models differ in following customization instructions. Their adjustments rarely align systematically with recipients’ backgrounds and do not improve persuasion overall in the human study.

title: Unheard Voices: The Importance of Intersectionality in Responsiveness and the Systematic Ignoring of Black Men by Elected Officials
authors: Ethan C. Busby, Andrew Ifedapo Thompson, Tomo Vierbuchen, and Suzy Yi
summary: A large-scale experiment with U.S. local elected officials finds that Black men were systematically ignored, regardless of the message they sent, highlighting the importance of intersectional theories of responsiveness.

title: Do They Even Care? Empirical Evidence for the Importance of Listening in Democracy
authors: Ethan C. Busby, Andrew Ifedapo Thompson, and Suzy Yi
summary: Citizens frequently define listening as fair consideration. A conjoint experiment shows that people respond positively when elected officials listen, even when other familiar predictors such as shared partisanship are held in view.

title: Testing Theories of Political Persuasion Using Artificial Intelligence
authors: Lisa P. Argyle, Ethan C. Busby, Joshua R. Gubler, Alex Lyman, Justin Olcott, Jackson Pond, and David Wingate
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122 (18): e2412815122
summary: Two survey experiments use generative AI to test theories of persuasion. AI-generated counterattitudinal messages changed some attitudes, but customization and interaction were not consistently more persuasive than a generic message.

title: Balancing Large Language Model Alignment and Algorithmic Fidelity in Social Science Research
authors: Alex Lyman, Bryce Hepner, Lisa P. Argyle, Ethan C. Busby, Joshua R. Gubler, and David Wingate
summary: The study compares aligned and unaligned open-source language models with human responses. It shows that alignment affects simulated attitudes in predictable ways and that model choice matters for social-science research.

title: Introduction: Progress and Promise in Political Psychology
authors: Ethan C. Busby, Christopher F. Karpowitz, and Cara J. Wong
venue: Handbook of Innovations in Political Psychology, 1–9
summary: An introduction to a handbook on how political psychology can respond to democratic strain, technological change, and new questions about political behavior.

title: Populism and Misinformation
authors: Nina Wiesehomeier, Ethan C. Busby, and D. J. Flynn
venue: The Ideational Approach to Populism, Volume II: Consequences and Mitigation
summary: A chapter on how populism can create problems for democracy, including affective polarization, weakened institutions, and harmful policy responses.

title: The Ideational Approach
authors: Ethan C. Busby, Angelos Chryssogelos, Eliza Tanner Hawkins, Kirk A. Hawkins, Levente Littvay, and Nina Wiesehomeier
venue: The Ideational Approach to Populism, Volume II
summary: A chapter explaining the ideational approach to populism and its relevance for understanding contemporary threats to democratic institutions.

title: The Political Psychology of Cancel Culture: Value Framing or Group Identity?
authors: Elle Diether, Suzy Yi, Lisa P. Argyle, and Ethan C. Busby
summary: Across survey data and experiments, partisanship strongly shapes how Americans understand and evaluate behaviors labeled cancel culture, while value framing has a weaker effect.

title: Changing Stereotypes of Partisans in the Trump Era
authors: Ethan C. Busby, Adam J. Howat, and C. Daniel Myers
summary: Comparing 2016 and 2021 responses, the study finds partisan stereotypes became less group- and issue-based and more focused on personal traits during the Trump era.

title: Defending the Dog Whistle: The Role of Justifications in Racial Messaging
authors: Andrew Ifedapo Thompson and Ethan C. Busby
summary: Survey experiments examine how justifications can reduce the political costs of racialized messages while preserving support among racially resentful White respondents.

title: Leveraging AI for Democratic Discourse: Chat Interventions Can Improve Online Political Conversations at Scale
authors: Lisa P. Argyle, Christopher A. Bail, Ethan C. Busby, Joshua R. Gubler, Thomas Howe, Christopher Rytting, Taylor Sorensen, and David Wingate
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 120 (41): e2311627120
summary: Evidence-based AI suggestions improved reported conversation quality, democratic reciprocity, and tone without systematically changing the content of conversations or policy attitudes.

title: Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples
authors: Lisa P. Argyle, Ethan C. Busby, Nancy Fulda, Joshua R. Gubler, Christopher Rytting, and David Wingate
summary: The study proposes that language models can simulate specific human subpopulations when conditioned on detailed demographic backstories, while emphasizing the need to evaluate algorithmic fidelity carefully.

title: Perceptions of Extremism among the American Public and Elected Officials
authors: Ethan C. Busby
summary: Americans and elected officials use ideas about spatial extremity and unwillingness to listen when defining extremism, but they often apply those standards unevenly across political camps.

title: Should You Stay Away from Strangers? Experiments on the Political Consequences of Intergroup Contact
authors: Ethan C. Busby
summary: A book-length study of how different forms of intergroup contact affect political attitudes, including when difficult communication produces backlash rather than harmony.

title: The Partisan Next Door: Stereotypes of Party Supporters and Consequences for Polarization in America
authors: Ethan C. Busby, Adam J. Howat, Jacob E. Rothschild, and Richard M. Shafranek
venue: Cambridge University Press, Elements in American Politics
summary: The book shows that images of ordinary partisans—especially trait-based images—shape affective and ideological polarization, while instrumental views may create room for compromise.

title: Framing and Blame Attribution in Populist Rhetoric
authors: Ethan C. Busby, Joshua R. Gubler, and Kirk A. Hawkins
summary: Dispositional blame frames activate latent populist attitudes more than situational frames, with downstream consequences for candidate support.

title: Pigeonholing Partisans: Stereotypes of Party Supporters and Partisan Polarization
authors: Jacob E. Rothschild, Adam J. Howat, Richard M. Shafranek, and Ethan C. Busby
summary: People describe partisans in terms of groups, issues, and traits. Trait-based stereotypes are especially associated with affective and ideological polarization.

title: Activating Populist Attitudes: The Role of Corruption
authors: Ethan C. Busby, David Doyle, Kirk A. Hawkins, and Nina Wiesehomeier
summary: The chapter examines how intentional misconduct and corruption can activate populist responses, especially when corruption is understood as widespread.

title: Studying Framing Effects on Political Preferences: Existing Research and Lingering Questions
authors: Ethan C. Busby, D. J. Flynn, James N. Druckman, and P. D’Angelo
summary: A review of framing-effects research that identifies strengths, limitations, and open questions about how political messages shape preferences.

title: Football and Public Opinion: A Partial Replication and Extension
authors: Ethan C. Busby and James N. Druckman
summary: A partial replication suggests that irrelevant events can affect some political attitudes, but the effect is constrained to particular outcomes and may be short-lived.

title: The Political Relevance of Irrelevant Events
authors: Ethan C. Busby, James N. Druckman, and Alexandria Fredendall
summary: An experiment finds that a sporting event can affect presidential approval, likely through mood, while emphasizing the importance of identifying when irrelevant-event effects occur.
